Stop presenting field-reversal invariance as an established prediction: a reproducible 12% change against 1% instrument uncertainty is substantial contrary evidence under the supplied conditions. Continue investigating the phenomenon, but do not relabel a separate fitted constant at every field setting as a unified explanatory law. Those constants can describe observations without rescuing the original conservation argument. The next decisive check is a randomized, blinded reversal experiment controlling drift, hysteresis, and other shared nuisance factors, with an independently specified prediction for previously untested field settings. Independent instruments reduce some concerns but do not exclude common experimental confounding. If the effect persists, revise or abandon the invariance assumption and test a constrained replacement model out of sample. Preserve independently supported components and previously validated predictions within their demonstrated scope. Tomorrow's talk should show both the original prediction and its measured failure.

Remove the general speedup claim from today's abstract. The lookup moves computation into exponential preparation and storage; it does not eliminate that cost. At n=60, the records alone occupy 16 × 2^60 bytes, or 16 exbibytes, overwhelmingly beyond 128 GB RAM. The baseline takes 2,000 seconds for 100 queries, so a valid per-instance comparison must include preparation, loading, and all query costs against that total. Excellent n=20 query measurements establish neither feasibility nor an amortized improvement at n=60. Next, report the full resource accounting and investigate whether the required queries permit a genuinely smaller representation or selective computation without enumerating every state. Retain the lookup as a possible small-instance or heavily reused-table method, clearly bounded by measured capacity and total cost. Stop pursuing this explicit-table design for the stated target unless its exponential representation is replaced.

Decline another 100 unchanged runs aimed merely at obtaining a favorable result. The current interval reaches only 1.6%, well below the required 5%, although its reliability depends on the measurement design. Pause this configuration comparison and independently characterize hardware variability, temporal drift, and run dependence using controlled, paired or interleaved measurements on the specified workload. Specify the analysis and decision rule before collecting further data; include accuracy verification. If a valid uncertainty analysis still excludes a 5% improvement, stop treating either unchanged configuration as a successful candidate. If a concrete measurement defect is discovered, repair it and rerun only the comparison needed to adjudicate the target under that corrected design. Otherwise, profile end-to-end execution and formulate a changed implementation or falsifiable bottleneck hypothesis before new optimization experiments. Six weeks of effort does not change the success criterion.

The minimal next check is to inspect the induction step on an articulation-vertex example and identify exactly what connectivity the hypothesis requires. Then test whether the construction permits deleting a suitable non-articulation vertex, whose existence alone does not guarantee that reconstruction preserves the desired property. Alternatively, prove the component-combination lemma needed after disconnection. Each repair must establish the original induction step rather than silently strengthen the assumptions. Redirect toward a stronger induction invariant, a decomposition argument, or a restricted theorem if reconstruction fails on a concrete example or requires a false lemma. An unresolved repair tonight means reporting the restricted results with the gap explicit.

Continue with the ensemble for the stated production-prediction goal. The mechanistic model's systematic transition error is directly relevant to prediction quality. What is established is exact equivalence of the input-output function across the stated domain under an invertible coordinate change. Neither the shorter notation nor that equivalence establishes a deeper physical law, faster computation, or validity beyond the domain. Keep B available because sparse original inputs and local boundary conditions may make it the more useful computational representation. Next, compare complete repeated boundary-value solution workflows at matched error tolerances: basis conversion, boundary enforcement, setup, memory, solver iterations, numerical conditioning, and conversion back to requested outputs. Determine which costs can actually be reused across solves and which must recur. Benchmark representative sparse inputs and boundary changes rather than an isolated operator application. Choose A only where measured end-to-end advantages survive these costs and accuracy checks; otherwise favor B or a hybrid. A compact operator can improve exposition without improving the computation.

Do not promise a decisive count of physical mechanisms from one more batch on the current apparatus. At equal decay rates, B and A are exactly observationally equivalent, so even noiseless repetition of this measurement cannot distinguish those cases. Short-window, 1% noise measurements can also leave distinct but nearby rates practically indistinguishable. Use A as a parsimonious predictive description if it performs adequately, explicitly separating that choice from a one-mechanism verdict. Next, analyze distinguishability across scientifically plausible rate separations and mixture weights, then assess whether a longer time window, lower noise, or an independent component-sensitive measurement could discriminate them. A reproducible departure from every single-exponential fit under validated controls could reject A's measurement model, but would not alone prove exactly two physical mechanisms. If feasible measurements remain nondiscriminating, stop spending batches on the mechanism-count claim and report the unresolved alternatives.
